analysis.one_liner: Caps what drug makers can charge for prescription drugs, tying US prices to prices in 11 other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap US prescription drug prices using prices from other countries never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Health and Human Services Department to set a maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the median price charged in 11 reference countries like Japan, Germany, France, and Canada. Those caps would apply to Medicare, Medicaid, the children's health program, military and veterans' health coverage, federal employees' insurance, and Indian health programs — and drug makers would have to offer the same price to uninsured people and people with private insurance. Companies that overcharged would owe a penalty of five times the excess, with the money going to federal drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and other people on Medicare and Medicaid, military families, veterans, federal workers, uninsured patients, and people with employer or private insurance, all of whom pay US drug prices that are often several times higher than the same drugs sell for in other wealthy countries.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the retail price of every prescription drug sold through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian health programs at a reference price set by HHS [S3].

Sets the reference price at the median list price among 11 peer countries (Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Sweden), or a value-based price where foreign data is unavailable [S3].
Requires manufacturers to offer drugs at the reference price to everyone — uninsured people and people with private or employer insurance — not just government programs [S3].
Penalizes overcharging at five times the excess revenue collected, with the penalties transferred to the NIH to fund drug research and development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to charge US buyers prices far above what they charge in other countries, and would face civil penalties for overcharging federal programs.

drawbacks.text: The price caps apply to generic drugs as well as brand-name ones, and a hard cap tied to foreign prices could leave manufacturers with little room to raise prices even when their production costs rise, which an honest supporter would acknowledge as a risk to supply [S3].

Where pricing data is not available in at least three reference countries, the price would be set by HHS judgment about a drug's value and research costs, a judgment-heavy process that could be slow, contested, and inconsistent from drug to drug [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and direct: prescription drugs in the US routinely sell for several times the prices paid in peer countries, and this bill would have extended government-negotiated-style caps beyond federal programs to uninsured and privately insured patients. The main costs fall on drug manufacturers rather than on patients, though the blunt foreign-median cap and judgment-based pricing for drugs without comparable foreign data are real design risks. On balance, the help to people paying high drug prices outweighs the acknowledged design flaws.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no further action on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on April 22, 2021, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee — the only action the chamber ever took on it [S5].
The committee never held a hearing or markup, the full Senate never voted, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they keep charging US patients and federal programs prices well above what they charge in other wealthy countries, with no penalty. Patients who pay those prices — including Medicare beneficiaries and the uninsured — are the ones who bear the cost of the bill dying.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and the Democratic-run committee and Senate never acted on it; no vote was ever recorded to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would cap their US prices at the median of 11 peer countries across all federal health programs and require the same price for uninsured and privately insured patients, with penalties of five times the overcharge. The US market is where these companies earn their highest prices, so blocking the bill preserved that premium pricing against ordinary patients and taxpayers.
The reference prices apply to generics too, but generic prices are generally low already, so most would see little change; the cap could squeeze margins on a subset of higher-priced generics.

industries.industry: Public and private health insurers and plans (Medicare, Medicaid, employer plans)
industries.note: Lower drug list prices would reduce what plans and government programs pay, and the requirement that plan coverage plus cost-sharing not exceed the reference price would push savings toward patients.
